item.title: Orthogonal Scores and Double/Debiased Machine Learning for Possibly Misspecified GMM
item.description: arXiv:2611.17578v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop Neyman orthogonal scores for GMM models that remain valid when the moment conditions may fail to hold. Existing score constructions typically require the moment conditions to hold exactly, which may fail in over-identified models, where the number of moment functions exceeds the number of parameters. We construct \emph{misspecification-robust} orthogonal score that has a closed form; it is the conventional orthogonal score plus adjustment terms, for the estimation of the Jacobian and of the weighting matrix, which are proportional to the population moment and vanish under correct specification. The moment functions may depend on nonparametric or machine learning first steps, and we show that double/debiased machine learning (DML) combined with the proposed scores and cross-fitting provides uniformly valid inference for a low-dimensional GMM estimand, while the conventional DML standard errors are inconsistent when the moment conditions fail. We illustrate the results in the partially linear instrumental variables (PLIV) model and in the local average treatment effects (LATE) model with multiple instruments.
item.dc:creator: Byunghoon Kang

item.title: Random Utility Models in the Consumption-Budget Setting: Vertex and Network-Flow Characterizations
item.description: arXiv:2611.17692v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This note supplements our paper \textit{Alternative Computational Formulations for Testing Discrete-Choice Random Utility Models: Half-Space and Network-Flow Formulations} and serves two purposes: 1. We clarify the conceptual distinctions between two classes of random utility models (RUM): those in the consumption-budget setting \citep{kitamura2019nonparametric} (hereafter KS) and those in the finite-alternative setting (e.g., Chapter~7 of \cite{chambers2016revealed}). In particular, we show (Theorem 1) that each rational type, as defined in KS, can be obtained as a coordinate projection of the deterministic choice vector induced by a strict preference ranking that satisfies what we call a patch-monotonicity condition. 2. We generalize the network-flow characterization for finite-alternative RUM in \cite{fiorini2004short} to the consumption-budget setting (Theorem 2). Specifically, we show that a vector of choice probabilities in the consumption-budget setting is rationalizable in the KS sense if and only if it is the image of a unit flow on a multi-arc powerset digraph under a fixed linear map. The key distinction is that our digraph allows multiple arcs between the same pair of nodes, whereas the digraph in Fiorini has at most one arc between any pair of nodes.
item.dc:creator: Haoge Chang, Kota Saito, Mingxi Zhu

item.title: Positive Weights Do Not Certify TWFE Inference: A Design Diagnostic under Treatment-Effect Heterogeneity
item.description: arXiv:2611.18116v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conventional two-way fixed-effects (TWFE) inference need not be uniformly adequate even when all treatment weights are positive. Under a local treatment-effect drift, the statistic for the equally weighted treated-cell effect has worst-case mean shift $(c/q)\Gamma$, where $\Gamma=\sqrt{N_1}\|w-u\|_2$ is design-only and $q$ is the cluster-score noise scale. Projection matches the exposure to cohort, event-time, additive, and saturated group-time pilots; when residualized treatment is constant within treated group-time cells, $\Gamma_{\mathrm{gt}}=\Gamma$. A direct score estimator is feasible with fixed panel length as clusters grow. Because a debiased quadratic pilot is nonregular at zero, we use two regular one-sided procedures: a reverse-triangle multiplier lower bound to detect unsafe envelopes and covariance-aware noncentral-$\chi^2$ inversion to certify adequacy. At $5\%$ nominal size with a five-point tolerance, the shift threshold is $0.652$. In the Callaway--Sant'Anna minimum-wage panel, where every treated-cell weight is positive, the saturated $95\%$ lower shift bound is $0.793$, so conventional inference is not uniformly certified. A complementary Brazilian property-tax reanalysis with $2{,}840$ municipalities withholds certification in all four classes; its smallest lower bound is $1.040$. Under the maintained many-cluster approximation, castle-doctrine homicide passes for additive cohort-plus-event-time heterogeneity with a $95\%$ upper bound of $0.236$; its saturated covariance lacks one required rank. Divorce is inconclusive. These envelopes are not predictions of realized rejection. The diagnostic separates point correction, uniform exposure, and statistically warranted certification.
item.dc:creator: Stanis{\l}aw M. S. Halkiewicz

item.title: Broken Adaptive Ridge in High-Dimensional Vector Autoregressions
item.description: arXiv:2611.18227v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study regularized estimation in high-dimensional vector autoregressions under physical dependence and row-wise approximate sparsity using the Broken Adaptive Ridge (BAR) estimator. BAR is an iteratively reweighted Ridge procedure whose fixed-point first-order conditions imply a coordinatewise thresholding rule that produces exact zeros. We show that the BAR estimation error can be analyzed on the union of the population support above the BAR threshold and the support selected in the sample. The size of this union can be controlled at the rate implied by approximate sparsity, allowing us to establish the required restricted-curvature condition and derive L1, L2, and prediction error rates when the number of regressors grows polynomially with the sample size and may exceed it. Under exact sparsity, the resulting rates recover the familiar rates for sparse high-dimensional estimation. Monte Carlo experiments across a range of high-dimensional VAR designs show that BAR delivers strong estimation and forecasting performance, and retains a high share of relevant coefficients relative to Lasso, adaptive Lasso, and SCAD. An application to U.S. inflation forecasting using FRED-MD shows particularly strong performance at the one-month horizon.
item.dc:creator: Gianluca Cubadda, Luca Margaritella, Orest Prifti

item.title: Estimating a Rational Inattention Discrete Choice Model: A Semiparametric Approach
item.description: arXiv:2611.18479v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: People's choices depend on both the payoffs of the available options and what they learn about those payoffs before deciding. This paper shows how choice data identify both unobserved payoff heterogeneity and the cost of information acquisition in a rational inattention discrete-choice model. I establish conditions for semiparametric point identification using exogenous payoff and information-cost shifters, without imposing parametric forms on the taste-shock distribution or on how the unit cost of information varies with observed characteristics. In the model with binary choice, I construct an unobserved choice threshold whose cumulative distribution function is the choice probability as a function of the payoff shifter. Moments of this threshold identify the payoff coefficients and the unit cost of information at each value of the information-cost shifter. A deconvolution argument then identifies the taste-shock distribution. I then extend identification to the model with multinomial choice. To estimate the model, I propose a sieve minimum-distance estimator based on observed market shares and establish its consistency. For inference, I construct confidence regions by test inversion because binding parameter constraints can make the estimator's limiting distribution nonnormal. In an application to Amazon Mechanical Turk, model counterfactuals show that lower unit costs of information raise the average task-taking probability and reduce wage elasticity.
item.dc:creator: Hanqi Wang

item.title: Correlation Between Nighttime Light and Various Statistical Indicators in Japan
item.description: arXiv:2609.33861v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This manuscript is an English translation and extended version of a paper originally published in Japanese(otomo 2021) Recent years have seen a rapid expansion in applying satellite remote sensing and big data to economic analysis. In particular, satellite-observed nighttime light intensity has proven to be closely correlated with key socio-economic indicators, including gross domestic product, employment rates, population density, and educational attainment across countries. In this paper, I first outline the methodology for calculating regional nightlight intensity across Japanese prefectures and municipalities. Next, to evaluate the versatility of nightlight data, I examine the relationship between city-level nightlight intensity and various public socio-economic metrics, using Japan as a case study. The findings suggest that nightlight intensity can serve as a effective proxy for these diverse indicators. Finally, I explore the potential of nightlight data for enabling rapid economic impact assessments during sudden social disruptions, such as the COVID-19 pandemic.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Theory and Applications of GIS, Vol. 29, No. 1, pp. 23-28, 2021
item.dc:creator: Shoichi Otomo

item.title: Making Experiment Results Comparable through Sitewide Impact Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2611.18411v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Roblox spans many product surfaces-discovery, the virtual economy, creator tools-that differ sharply in reach and in how much the affected population contributes to any sitewide metric. A randomized experiment shows whether a treatment works for the users in its sample, but this experiment lift is not comparable across surfaces, because surfaces differ in reach and in their contribution to sitewide metrics. The quantity a strategic decision needs is a counterfactual-how much an aggregated sitewide metric (e.g., total platform play time) would move if the treatment reached 100% of its target population, which may be only part of the sitewide population, during the measurement period. We call this sitewide impact. Its scaling factor, which we call the coverage factor, combines the reach and the target population's contribution to the sitewide metric under no treatment. Hence a low-reach surface whose users carry much of the metric could outrank a high-reach surface whose users carry little. We develop two estimators under this framing: one for difference-in-means metrics and one for variant-level ratio metrics (a metric defined as a ratio of two population aggregates). Empirically, experiment lift is a poor proxy for sitewide impact-across 139 experiments that are statistically significant on time spent, the Spearman rank correlation between the two is 0.20, and 5 of the 10 largest experiment lifts are among the 10 largest sitewide impacts. We validate the estimator with A/A tests and against a long-term holdout, and apply it to cross-domain prioritization and attributing year-over-year growth to shipped innovations.
item.dc:creator: Xiaochen Zhang, Wenjing Zheng, Xingye Kang, Vamsi Manthena

item.title: Constrained Stochastic Policy Targeting under Heterogeneous Partial Interference
item.description: arXiv:2611.18444v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Under heterogeneous interference, treating individuals with particular characteristics affects the population average outcome through their heterogeneous direct response to treatment and indirect effect on others, creating opportunities for efficient policy design. For instance, policymakers may minimize resource use by vaccinating individuals identified as superspreaders to achieve a target reduction in disease incidence. In such setting, we first study the problem of learning individualized stochastic treatment policies that minimize population average treatment probability subject to a prespecified outcome target. We propose an estimation approach based on a smooth surrogate for constraint violations and interference-aware inverse-probability-weighting or self-normalized estimators of the population average outcome, and establish finite-sample regret guarantees for both estimators. We also consider the complementary problem of maximizing the population average outcome subject to a constraint on average treatment probability. We apply the proposed methodology to a Colombian conditional cash transfer program aimed at improving school attendance. The application demonstrates that accounting for interference and individualizing treatment probabilities can reduce resource use relative to policies that ignore interference or impose homogeneous treatment probabilities.
item.dc:creator: Elena Dal Torrione, Chan Park, Laura Forastiere

item.title: Sensitivity Analysis for Linear Estimators
item.description: arXiv:2309.06305v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a framework for building sensitivity analyses for linear estimators. We measure the degree of identification failure by the change of measure between the observed distribution and a hypothetical target distribution under which a standard estimator would identify the parameter of interest. Under L_infinity bounds on that derivative, the identified set has closed-form sharp bounds that require no numerical optimization and that are computable and continuous when the derivative is unbounded, nesting Manski-type worst-case bounds and existing characterizations that require bounded changes of measure. The framework nests several selection models for average potential outcomes, yielding the established worst-case bounds of each design. The framework yields a new model family for regression discontinuity (RD) that delivers the first sensitivity analysis on the conditional average treatment effect under manipulation. We show that a bootstrap procedure yields valid confidence intervals. An empirical application shows that a modest restriction on manipulation delivers bounds far more informative than worst-case bounds.
item.dc:creator: Jacob Dorn, Luther Yap

item.title: Post-Selection Inference for Partially Identified Parameters
item.description: arXiv:2403.00422v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Partial identification of parameters such as average treatment effects, average partial effects and welfare is particularly common when using observational data and experimental data with imperfect compliance due to the endogeneity of individuals' treatment uptake. In this setting, the researcher is typically interested in a treatment or policy that is either selected from the estimated set of best-performers or arises from a data-dependent selection rule. In this paper, we develop new inference tools for partially-identified parameters chosen via these forms of selection. We develop three types of confidence intervals for data-dependent and partially-identified parameters, discuss how they apply to several examples of interest and prove their uniform asymptotic validity under weak assumptions.
item.dc:creator: Sukjin Han, Adam McCloskey

item.title: Approximating an Ideal Experiment with Induced Order Statistics
item.description: arXiv:2603.07255v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many economic questions concern the conditional distribution of an outcome at a fixed covariate value. We refer to observing i.i.d.\ draws from this distribution as an \emph{ideal experiment}, under which many statistical procedures admit exact, finite-sample guarantees. When the covariate is continuously distributed, however, this ideal experiment is unavailable. We provide a general method for approximating this ideal experiment using \emph{induced order statistics}, the outcomes attached to the nearest observed covariates. We derive explicit bounds on the approximation error in Hellinger and total variation distances. These bounds quantify how local approximation errors accumulate as the nearest-neighbor sample grows and provide a unified way to transfer rejection and coverage guarantees across statistical procedures. Under quadratic mean differentiability and local regularity of the covariate distribution, the bounds apply to both interior and boundary conditioning points and give explicit conditions on the growth of the nearest-neighbor sample. We illustrate the approach in four distinct applications: covariate balance testing in regression discontinuity designs, conditional quantile inference, conformal prediction at a fixed covariate value, and policy-irrelevance testing under network interference.
item.dc:creator: Federico A. Bugni, Ivan A. Canay, Deborah Kim

item.title: Local Asymptotic Power of Honest Confidence Intervals
item.description: arXiv:2607.10558v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Honest or bias-aware confidence intervals, conservative against untestable bias, are now standard in DiD, IV, RD, and factor models. This paper characterises the local power of their tests, which has three regimes set by the bias bound's rate relative to the sampling rate. A bound vanishing faster than the standard error costs nothing, one of the same order costs a bounded amount, and a dominating bound, typical at the parametric rate, leaves zero local power. This loss is intrinsic to honesty, and the standard bias-aware interval is rate-optimal. The paper recommends reporting the power ``dead zone'' half-width alongside bias-aware intervals.
item.dc:creator: Hugo Freeman

item.title: Who Is Prioritized? Current Need versus Predicted Gains in China's Dibao Allocation: Evidence from a Revealed-Allocation Model
item.description: arXiv:2609.08411v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Using the 2017--2021 China Household Finance Survey panel and a sample of 3,102 households that did not receive Dibao in 2017, this paper applies the BBK revealed-allocation model to examine how household economic circumstances and predicted policy gains explain observed Dibao receipt in China. We find that household income is the allocation criterion most difficult to substitute with other factors. When all gain-adjustment terms are positive, constraining the income-rank coefficient to be nonnegative reduces the model's original improvement in fit by approximately 33.6\%; by contrast, setting both predicted-gain coefficients for food consumption and education spending to zero still preserves approximately 95.6\% of that improvement. These results indicate that observed Dibao allocation places greater emphasis on prioritizing households facing current livelihood hardship than on pursuing predictable short-run improvements in expenditure outcomes. This allocation orientation reflects the trade-off in social assistance between basic-livelihood protection and expected policy gains and offers a new perspective on the potential long-run social-welfare value of basic-livelihood protection.
item.dc:creator: Haojie Liu, Jiyuan Ling, Zihan Lin

item.title: Intentionally Overidentifying Local Projections
item.description: arXiv:2610.13269v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Local projections (LPs) have become a standard tool for estimating dynamic effects in macroeconomics and are typically implemented using ordinary least squares (OLS) for a given lag order. We propose an alternative approach that exploits additional lags as excluded instrumental variables (IVs). Under a finite-order model with martingale-difference shocks, the resulting (optimally weighted) IV estimator is never asymptotically less efficient than OLS and, as we show, can deliver substantial efficiency gains when data are persistent. For the unit-root AR(1) data with i.i.d. errors, our baseline IV estimator (with one overidentifying restriction) has asymptotic variance $2-h^{-1}$, compared with $h$, the asymptotic variance of the OLS lag-augmented estimator in Montiel Olea and Plagborg-M{\o}ller (2021), for an integer propagation horizon $h$. We then develop IV-based LP inference that is robust to unknown persistence and moderate local model misspecification. We also characterize the trade-off between the degree of misspecification and the number of additional lag controls. Through simulations and an empirical application, we demonstrate that the proposed method can yield meaningfully shorter confidence intervals for impulse responses than OLS in finite samples.
item.dc:creator: Junjie Guo, Endong Wang, Ke-Li Xu

item.title: Benefits and Costs of Adaptive Sampling
item.description: arXiv:2604.24652v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multi-armed bandits are widely used for sequential experimentation in clinical trials, public policy treatment, recommendation systems, and online platforms. While regret minimization and valid inference from adaptively collected data have each been studied individually, one question remains: when does adaptivity \emph{improve estimation precision} relative to uniform designs, and how should inference be balanced against the online cost of experimentation? We first study arm-level mean estimation under mean-squared-error (MSE) objectives. We characterize when an adaptive Neyman allocation, which allocates samples according to arm variance, yields strict MSE improvements over uniform sampling in finite samples. When there is variance heterogeneity across arms, these improvements arise at modest sample sizes, clarifying that adaptivity can be preferable for inference not only asymptotically, but also in finite-sample settings. We then study a joint inference--regret objective that accounts for the cost of assigning units to inferior arms during experimentation. We propose three policies: the Plug-in Oracle Rate Policy, Static-Allocation Rate Policy, and Neyman-Adaptive Rate Policy, all of which attain the oracle-optimal asymptotic rate. The latter two offer computationally efficient and easy-to-implement alternatives by combining existing regret-minimizing algorithms with inference-oriented sampling through closed-form mixing rules, avoiding repeated numerical optimization while being managerially interpretable. We compare their finite-sample statistical performance through simulations and empirically calibrated applications. The results highlight the relative strengths of our policies across instances and their tradeoffs between joint inference--regret performance and computational cost.
item.dc:creator: Yu-Shiou Willy Lin, Dae Woong Ham, Iavor Bojinov
